abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.
title: How to "train" a surgeon? Benchmarking generalist agents in surgical scene understanding

abstract: Pre-training code language models relies on massive code corpora usually streamed over the internet. However, researchers rarely need a multi-terabyte archive in its entirety; instead, their workflow centers on curated subsets: selecting well-documented files, filtering out repetitive boilerplate, auditing for benchmark contamination, or retrieving specific code patterns. Yet, because modern corpora are typically published as file pointers and basic attributes rather than source text, no general structural layer exists to select which files to download: curating a subset requires downloading and parsing millions of files first just to discard most of them. We present SWHForest, an open-source framework and public dataset that provides this missing structural layer for any pointer-based corpus without redistributing source code. A single pass over the archive parses each file into an AST and immediately discards the source text, keeping only its structural summary. Queried locally or exposed by archive providers as a server-side filtering API, SWHForest selects matching files first (via SQL or index intersection) and downloads only surviving candidates. Across the ten largest languages of Stack-Edu (52.1M unique files, 341M definitions), SWHForest answers curation queries in milliseconds while cutting downloads by 46-72%, reducing live structural searches from hours of per-language streaming to seconds or minutes.
title: SWHForest: A Structural Curation and Search Layer for Large-Scale Code Corpora

abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.
title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers

abstract: The order in which propagators are executed can substantially affect the performance of constraint programming solvers, yet propagator priorities are typically determined by fixed, manually designed heuristics. In this work, we explore learning instance-dependent propagator priorities from static problem features. We formulate the task as a learning-to-rank problem, addressing the challenge that the quality of a priority assignment can be measured through solver runtime, while the desired priorities of individual propagators are not directly observable. A self-attention-based model jointly scores the propagators present in an instance and is trained using pairwise preferences derived from solver runtimes measured under randomized propagator priority assignments, with a Plackett-Luce-based ranking objective. Predicted rankings are mapped to the discrete priority levels of the Choco solver before search begins, without modifying its propagation or search procedures. We evaluate the approach on XCSP3 instances and demonstrate that propagator ordering can have a substantial impact on solving time. On a test set of 698 instances, picked out as most difficult by problem class, the learned priorities increase the number of solved instances from 634 to 654, reduce median solver runtime by 27.93%, and reduce aggregate penalized runtime (PAR1) by 12.65% compared with Choco's default priorities. We further observe that improvements vary across problem classes and show that a simple policy selecting between learned and default priorities further increases the number of solved instances. These results demonstrate the potential of learning instance-dependent propagator priorities to improve constraint programming performance, particularly on difficult instances.
title: Learning to Rank Propagators in Constraint Programming

abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd
title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?

abstract: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.
title: Semantically Aligned KV Cache Compression for Efficient Agentic Autoregressive Video Generation

abstract: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.
title: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training

abstract: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.
title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations

abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: My Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge

abstract: Audio deepfake detectors trained with known synthesis attacks can learn generator-specific shortcuts that fail as synthesis systems and acoustic conditions evolve. We investigate an attack-free alternative: a normality model trained exclusively on bona fide speech, which scores synthetic audio by its deviation from authentic representations. We propose MLN-WavLM, a method that applies shrinkage-Mahalanobis modeling to pooled hidden states from a frozen large-scale, pre-trained speech processing WavLM Base+ architecture. Evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA, our best attack-free variant achieves an 8.45\% Equal Error Rate (EER), closely tracking a fully supervised WavLM-HM-Conformer baseline (7.86%). However, when subjected to the ASVspoof 2021 DF domain shift, performance drops to 22.12% EER, exposing vulnerabilities in the bona-fide-calibrated operating point. Layer-wise analysis reveals that early WavLM representations dominate the ensemble. To test real-world viability, we simulated deployment streams using unlabeled threshold adaptation. While robust median/MAD recalibration easily handles in-domain contamination up to 10%, recalibrating under the 2021 DF domain shift triggers a total collapse of low-FPR recall. We conclude that while frozen source-domain normality can effectively rank deepfakes, it does not yield a stable open-world decision rule, and downstream threshold adaptation cannot rescue upstream ranking degradation.
title: When Normality Shifts: Multi-Level WavLM Modeling for Open-World Audio Deepfake Detection

abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.
title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks

abstract: Generating accurate CAD models requires substantial engineering expertise and careful control of geometry, topology, and mechanical constraints. Text-to-CAD aims to simplify this process, but current LLM-based methods often generate CAD programs directly. Language models remain unreliable when producing long code while coordinating coupled geometric, topological, and dimensional constraints. Consequently, executable programs may still produce structurally incorrect models, which execution rate and rendered appearance may fail to reveal. To address these limitations, we propose GOPR-CAD, an agentic Text-to-CAD pipeline based on Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning. A language model acts as a decision agent over encapsulated CAD operations and progressively constructs an executable operation graph, which a deterministic compiler converts into the final CAD model. This separation requires no additional training and supports different language models. To evaluate structural fidelity, we construct MHCAD, a benchmark of 300 standard mechanical part requirements derived from Machinery's Handbook. Their explicit structures enable reference-free STEP/B-rep evaluation. GOPR-CAD achieves 82.7% Structural Yield on MHCAD, and 87.2% Structural Yield on an external CADPrompt subset.
title: GOPR-CAD: Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning for CAD Generation

abstract: The small open embedder EmbeddingGemma-300M, used as released, finds the right passage first for only 51.7% to 60.8% of Belebele questions in Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz. We present Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M, one model for all four languages. It is our Tajik fine-tune of EmbeddingGemma-300M, trained for one more epoch on 279,904 pairs: questions in Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz that our own language model wrote about source passages, a Tajik refresher, and English and Russian replay. On Belebele, recall@1 rises by 14.4 to 26.0 points in each language, to between 75.2% and 77.7%. Against single-language models trained with the same settings, the one model stays within 2.8 points at recall@1 in Kazakh, Uzbek and Tajik, with overlapping recall@10 intervals, though it also had more training. It keeps the Tajik law recall@10 of its starting point (92.2 against 92.4) but loses 4.4 points of law recall@1. A model trained on one of these languages also improves the others on Belebele, but less than training on them. The model still trails the 560M XLM-RoBERTa embedders on Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz Belebele: the better of multilingual-e5-large-instruct and BGE-M3, used as released, is 9.4 to 10.2 points ahead at recall@1. Our scores of those released models agree with the published MTEB results within 2.4 points. Russian and English recall@1 fall by 3.0 and 4.2 points.
title: Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M: One Small Embedder for Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz

abstract: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.
title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation

abstract: In multi-institutional biomedical data analysis, comprehensive disease profiles are often fragmented across different data silos. Furthermore, local data distributions typically exhibit varying levels of granularity or even complex nested structures. Although Hierarchical Clustering (HC) is a powerful tool for exploring such data topologies, its cumbersome recursive process incurs prohibitive computational overhead and renders it highly susceptible to privacy leakage. This paper, therefore, introduces an efficient one-shot hierarchical FC framework that performs client-end (institutions) distribution exploration and server-end distribution aggregation through one-way prototype-level communication from clients to the server. Although the designed one-shot prototype transmission guarantees minimal computational overhead and mitigates privacy risks, it inevitably incurs information loss. To counteract this, a multi-granular competitive learning mechanism is proposed on the server to fuse the clusterlets, effectively maximizing the retention and mining of global distribution topologies under limited, one-way communication constraints. It turns out that the complex cluster distributions across clients can be efficiently explored, and extensive experiments comparing state-of-the-art methods on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework in balancing robust clustering, privacy preservation, and computational efficiency.
title: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering for Distributed Non-IID Biomedical Data Analysis

abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.
title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction

abstract: We present MicroSim, a system for binary code similarity detection that represents each function as a graph built from IDA Pro Hex-Rays microcode and compares such graphs with a contrastive Siamese graph neural network (GNN). We evaluate on the TREX cross-optimization benchmark, a corpus of 849,072 function-level microcode graphs spanning optimization levels -O0 through -O3, under a strict class-disjoint split in which no function key is shared between train and test. Under this protocol, MicroSim reaches 0.9972 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and 0.9762 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), outperforming Gemini (0.9332 ROC-AUC), SAFE (0.9752), and jTrans (0.9740) retrained on the same split, as well as a structure-free Bag-of-Words (BoW) baseline (0.9484). We analyze the gap between pair classification and ranked retrieval in graph transformers, showing that Cross-domain Similarity Local Scaling (CSLS) under unified tie-resolved evaluation raises GraphGPS mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.2542 to 0.2559 (R@1 = 0.1639, R@10 = 0.4561), strictly satisfying the theoretical MRR upper bound. Finally, over 5 seeds with equal compute, the pairwise cosine-embedding loss attains a slightly higher ROC-AUC (Δ = -0.0256, 95% confidence interval [-0.3282, +0.2770]), whereas the supervised-contrastive information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) loss is significantly better on thresholded classification and ranked retrieval.
title: MicroSim: Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Binary Code Similarity Detection

abstract: Existing evaluations often test persona expression rather than whether persona information persists in extended decision-making. We introduce THEATRON, a controlled benchmark that uses financial replay to evaluate persona persistence in long-horizon sequential decision-making. In these environments, models conditioned on fixed behavioral-finance personas observe shared daily market evidence and trajectory-specific account-state feedback and make sequential decisions over multi-month trajectories. We evaluate Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought persona injection across four LLMs, using cumulative-return and action trajectories to diagnose within-persona stability, cross-persona separability, and action collapse. Persona conditioning produces systematic behavioral shifts beyond a no-persona baseline, and persona-level separation generally exceeds the variation induced by semantically equivalent descriptions. Nevertheless, these shifts do not reliably form coherent persona-specific policies: apparently stable separation can arise from stereotyped action collapse, while diverse policies can exhibit noisy trajectory switching. These findings expose a gap between observable persona-induced behavior and persistent, context-sensitive persona-conditioned decision policies. Code and benchmark data are publicly available at: https://github.com/yuyan12138/theatron
title: THEATRON: A Benchmark for Evaluating Persona Persistence in Long-Horizon LLM Decision-Making

abstract: Many studies of animal vocalizations require clean recordings, but animals are usually recorded in the field, with background noise from weather, vehicles, and other animals. Animal vocalization denoising is challenged by the scarcity of clean training data and the extreme diversity of animal vocalizations. Classical spectral gates leave residual noise, especially without voice activity detection (VAD), while detector-free neural denoisers designed for bioacoustics remove less noise. We show that a general-purpose source separation foundation model, SAM-Audio, removes more noise than either of these types of methods, when used without training and prompted with time spans from a simple animal VAD. To turn this heavy method into a practical tool, we distill it into CallCleaner, a 19M-parameter denoiser that needs no detector and runs ~90x faster than real time on a laptop CPU. We find that SI-SDR has limited utility in our setting as it penalizes regenerated output and conflates noise removal with call fidelity, a trade-off our separate metrics reveal. CallCleaner leaves 11 dB less noise around the call than Biodenoising, the leading neural bioacoustic denoiser with public weights, and among fast, CPU-capable systems it pushes the Pareto frontier of noise removal vs. call fidelity, without requiring a detector. We release code and weights for CallCleaner, which enables fast, private, local denoising of single-caller recordings without specialized hardware.
title: CallCleaner: Lightweight Bioacoustic Denoising from an Audio Foundation Model

abstract: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.
title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions

abstract: We study stochastic bandits with reward-dependent delays, possibly infinite, whose reports omit the originating round. For each $c\in[0,1)$, Balanced Historical Optimism (BHO) has a delay term controlled by the largest suboptimal-arm quantile at level $1-cΔ_i$, without requiring optimal-arm reports. Lower bounds give an inverse-square slack cost in the logarithmic statistical regime and linear minimax regret at $c=1$. A family with growing $K$ forces worst-case regret $Ω(G\log K)$ for every learner, where $G=\max_iΔ_i h_i$ is the largest gap-weighted suboptimal cutoff. Pending-triggered balance preserves BHO's weighted-cutoff bound for $c<1$ and attains the historical-greedy exploration coefficient with deterministic rewards, a unique optimum and fixed bounded delays. Gap-weighted comparisons and experiments show when shared waiting helps and what balanced exploration costs.
title: Regret without Optimal-Arm Feedback under Reward-Dependent Delays

abstract: We describe the system submitted by Telefónica Innovación Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.
title: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track

abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.
title: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute

abstract: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).
title: JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Marcolli, Chomsky, and Berwick (2025; henceforth MCB) formulate the Merge operation of Minimalism on a Hopf algebra of Connes-Kreimer type, and claim that language and physics obey the same algebraic structure. This paper separates their program into the working hypothesis H, that Merge on workspaces can be described as a Hopf algebra, and the claim P placed on top of it, that language and physics obey the same principle, and examines the validity of H. MCB employs two coproducts in formulating Merge, corresponding to two different translations of movement (Internal Merge): $Δ_d$, which deletes the lower copy, and $Δ_c$, which leaves a trace. MCB uses the former in syntax and the latter at the syntax-semantics interface, but $Δ_d$ is not coassociative, and $Δ_c$ is not connected under the gradings MCB gives and, moreover, not coassociative as long as the labels of traces are retained. Consequently, MCB's algebra is not a Hopf algebra, and the Birkhoff factorization is not a consequence of the Hopf-algebra theorem but of a weaker statement that requires neither coassociativity nor connectedness. There are four ways to recover a Hopf algebra, but none of them can distinguish different traces, and hence none is compatible with Heim-Kratzer-style formal semantics, which reads traces as indexed variables. Thus H does not hold at present, and under the current formulation, making Minimalism a Hopf algebra and preserving its connection with formal semantics are mutually exclusive. Finally, we indicate three directions in which algebraic Minimalism may proceed.
title: Does Merge Form a Hopf Algebra? Coproducts, Traces, and the Prospects of Algebraic Minimalism

abstract: Due to the fundamental problem of causal inference -- the impossibility of observing counterfactual outcomes -- there is always a gap between the training goal (outcome, propensity) and the inference target (CATE, ATE). Traditional causal effect estimation revolves around setting assumptions, selecting identification strategies, and choosing causal estimators, while more recently, Causal Foundation Models (CFMs), built on Prior-Data-Fitted Networks (PFNs), ease this process by pretraining on massive synthetic prior datasets. Despite their success, such amortization makes causal inference less transparent, obscuring which assumptions the model implicitly relies on for a given dataset. The high diversity of real-world data-generating processes (DGPs) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) makes it hard to know, a priori, which causal inference strategy is compatible with a given dataset. In this work, we focus on this compatibility between an observational dataset and method-specific assumptions, and find that geometric characteristics of data embeddings -- specifically, the variogram -- provide a useful signal of whether a given causal estimation strategy is appropriate. We develop MoE-Learner, a mixture-of-causal-experts framework that embeds a dataset under multiple assumption-specific views and uses the variogram as a counterfactual-free router to assess each expert's validity. Rather than eliminating causal assumptions, this shifts their validation from a fixed, a priori choice to a criterion that can be checked directly from data geometry. MoE-Learner achieves the best average rank on benchmark datasets (IHDP, ACIC, Lalonde). Being orthogonal to (causal) foundation models, our method builds a bridge from data characteristics to causal estimation strategy rather than proposing another CFM.
title: Data-informed Adaptation of Foundation Models for Causal Effect Estimation

abstract: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.
title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents

abstract: Lookup-table (LUT)-based neural networks (NNs) offer a compelling path to ultra-low-latency inference on FPGAs. However, existing LUT-based neural networks have largely been restricted to MLP-style topologies, leaving structured vision and audio tasks underexplored. We present ConvLUT, a family of fully unrolled LUT-mappable convolutional architectures targeting the MLPerf Tiny benchmarks. It is comprised of a standard convolutional model built around a hierarchical tree of LUTs and a depthwise separable model following the MobileNet design philosophy. These architectures are enabled by four key contributions: a unified LUT-based convolutional framework supporting standard, depthwise, and pointwise convolutions under explicit fan-in constraints; a LUT-tree that addresses the $k^2c$ receptive field dimensionality bottleneck; a channel-partitioned LUT pooling layer that replaces conventional spatial pooling; and a hardware-aware iterative pruning strategy for stable convergence at scale. Evaluated on CIFAR-10, Visual Wake Words, and Keyword Spotting, ConvLUT achieves competitive accuracy with fully unrolled inference latencies below $\sim 50$ ns. On CIFAR-10 it reaches at least a $8844\times$ latency reduction over non-logic-based prior implementations, and outperforms existing MLP-style LUT-based models on the same task by at least $20$ pp in test accuracy.
title: ConvLUT: Rethinking Convolutional Architectures for Ultra-Low-Latency LUT-Based Inference

abstract: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of their own.
title: Review the Episodes, Refine the Lessons: Simple Memory Evolution for Embodied Agents

abstract: Amortized Bayesian experimental design (BED) enables real-time design strategies by shifting acquisition cost offline, but existing methods remain tied to the prior and task distribution they were trained on and cannot exploit additional information available at deployment. We introduce in-context amortized BED with unified knowledge encoding (IMBUE), a BED framework that admits external knowledge at deployment through a unified in-context interface. IMBUE accepts two forms of such knowledge without retraining, namely user-specified prior knowledge and observations from previous instances of the experiment. Both are encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with the accumulated observations by a shared Transformer, and a learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones. Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and remains close to the no-external baseline when it is not.
title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning

abstract: Understanding how an athlete moves can improve both technique and safety, yet outside the laboratory technique is still assessed by eye. We present a pipeline that detects named golf swing faults from ordinary video, without markers or calibration. Instead of learning end to end, it tracks body pose and the clubhead in a body-centered frame, and classifies the biomechanical quantities a coach would measure, such as the height of the clubhead above the swing plane, with shallow boosted trees. We demonstrate the approach on two common faults, coming over-the-top (OTT) and early-extension (EE). On 160 swings and 143 swings from public sources it detects OTT and EE with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.975 and 0.911 respectively. Because every feature is a biomechanical quantity a coach already uses, measured at a known phase of the downswing, each decision can be traced to the signals and the moments of the swing that drove it. The signals the model relies on most are the same ones a coach checks when diagnosing these faults. The pipeline processes phone video on a consumer laptop in seconds, so it could feasibly be developed into an app for golfers of all abilities and extended to other sports in which technique is judged against a biomechanical reference.
title: Detecting Common Golfing Faults Using AI and Video-Derived Biomechanical Features

abstract: Text- and goal-conditioned human-object interaction (HOI) provides an intuitive interface for specifying high-level intents in physics-based character animation. Mapping such intents to physically plausible, contact-rich behaviors naturally calls for a generative planner and a physics-based controller, yet existing planner-controller systems either execute plans open-loop or close the loop while keeping the planner fixed, so execution feedback never reshapes what is planned. We present InfCoiL, a closed-loop framework for physics-based HOI from coordinated planner-controller learning. InfCoiL couples a morphology-aware flow-matching planner with a unified multi-morphology controller through a shared morphology interface in an autoregressive plan-and-execute loop, and alternately fine-tunes both components with reinforcement learning from the same physical rollouts. To optimize the flow-matching planner online, we introduce Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which stochasticizes selected denoising transitions with channel-wise semantic covariance over heterogeneous HOI features and assigns group-relative, sequence-level rewards from complete closed-loop executions. On held-out OMOMO sequences, InfCoiL outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching task success and physical tracking accuracy. Project page: https://infcoil.github.io/
title: InfCoiL: Coordinated Planner-Controller Learning for Closed-Loop Physics-Based Human-Object Interaction

abstract: Real-world evolving networks are naturally modeled as temporal graphs (TGs), where capturing temporal dynamics is essential for predicting future graph properties that support downstream decision-making. Existing temporal graph methods have been developed primarily for single-task prediction, and little is known about their generalization across tasks or transfer to unseen networks. This leaves the challenge of multi-task graph property prediction in TGs largely open. We address this challenge by introducing Hydra, a novel architecture that integrates local connectivity features from temporal GNNs with a spectral learning module that captures global connectivity patterns. This design enables joint learning of local and global information under a multi-task objective. In multi-task classification, Hydra achieves an 8.9% relative gain in AUC over the strongest competitor. In multi-task regression, Hydra achieves competitive results in all three tasks, while obtaining the best results in two tasks with a 8.2% relative gain in MAE compared to the strongest baseline. Moreover, Hydra delivers these gains with a 22% reduction in training time compared to temporal transfer models. These results provide the first systematic evidence that multi-task transferable learning on temporal graphs is effective. By delivering consistent top-ranked performance, Hydra highlights multi-task training on temporal graphs as a promising direction toward adaptable foundation models for temporal graphs.
title: Hydra: Towards Transferable Multi-Task Learning on Temporal Graphs

abstract: World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K-PWM, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K-PWM couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K-PWM, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These results support structured probabilistic dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation.
title: K-PWM: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation

abstract: We propose a music inpainting technique combining similarity matching and a diffusion-based generative model to replace large segments of audio recordings with suitable alternatives. The proposed hybrid method, Similarity-Guided Diffusion Posterior Sampling (SimDPS), retrieves candidate replacement segments from the wider signal based on contextual similarity and uses them to guide the diffusion process toward coherent reconstructions. Being model-agnostic, the framework is compatible with any pre-trained diffusion model operating in either the waveform or latent domain. Objective evaluations demonstrate that SimDPS outperforms widely adopted RePaint and DPS methods across acoustic features and neural-embedding distance metrics. Subjective evaluations on multi-genre music datasets confirm that SimDPS enhances perceptual plausibility compared to previous diffusion-based methods and demonstrates robustness to poorly matched similarity candidates. These findings pave the way for improved music restoration and context-aware audio editing.
title: Music Inpainting With Similarity-Guided Latent Diffusion

abstract: Low-label transfer is often decided by a practical question: after a representation looks useful, how many labels are still needed to learn the downstream boundary? Transferability and probe-quality scores characterize global alignment, likelihood, margins, and calibration. Boundary-near target mass complements these diagnostics by measuring the ambiguous regions where scarce labels are most costly. We propose effective boundary complexity, a label-budget diagnostic for frozen representations and linear probes. It measures mass in a thin strip around the learned boundary and normalizes it by class balance, so dense ambiguous regions and predicted-class imbalance are both counted. We prove that, under a smooth representation map, density change and tangential surface change cancel at first order, leaving boundary-normal stretch or compression as the governing factor. This yields a cached-feature estimator that fits a probe on one split and counts independent held-out features near its boundary. Experiments support the diagnostic at three levels. Controlled transformations match the predicted law across 74 maps with 0.38% median relative error. On real frozen features, normal-direction changes move both measured boundary mass and label demand, while tangent controls preserve the first-order coefficient. A differentiable surrogate reduces measured complexity by 16-36% at matched top-1 utility. Finally, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet experiments support boundary mass as a second-stage diagnostic for near-tied representations. Five-way experiments show strong OvR-interface backbone-ranking agreement (Spearman 0.872), while acquisition experiments show high correlations between initial boundary mass and realized label budgets across three sampling policies (0.779-0.830). Code is available at https://github.com/qqaqq-code/boundary_mass.
title: Boundary Mass in Feature Space as a Label-Budget Diagnostic for Representations

abstract: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW's dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW's fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.
title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence

abstract: There is a well-established body of work demonstrating that individual machine learning (ML) algorithms can be manipulated or deceived. However, in many real-world systems, multiple ML algorithms are composed to enable automated decision-making, particularly in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). Often such systems use a composition of vision, planning, and other ML models to affect their internal state and ultimate take actions in the physical world. While there is a huge literature on the (in)security of ML algorithms, it is not immediately clear how an attacker might leverage their ability to trick individual learners when attacking the composition as a whole. We develop methods for creating an attack policy (a mapping from state to attack) for a data-manipulating attacker affecting a CPS or other state-machine-based AI compositions. We describe our framework, a basic threat model and corresponding methods for computing an optimal attack policy, as well as planned extensions. The goal of this work-in-progress paper is to stimulate conversation and forge new collaborations regarding the security of compositional learning.
title: Data Manipulation Attacks Against Machine Learning Integrated Cyber-Physical Systems

abstract: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.
title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module

abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
title: DriveFoundry: Co-Evolving Data and Model for Efficient Closed-Loop Iteration in Autonomous Driving

abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: llama.cpp's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against llama.cpp and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.
title: Ostinato: Fast CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents via Resident Experts in Every Forward Pass

abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.
title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer

abstract: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $τ$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.
title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction

abstract: Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors. Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks. Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision. Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.
title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification

abstract: Generative recommendation models represent items as sequences of discrete tokens known as semantic IDs. Existing approaches derive these identifiers using residual or hierarchical vector quantization, assuming that tokens carry independent semantic meaning across quantization levels. Revisiting this assumption, we argue that semantic IDs should behave as hierarchical paths where each token's meaning is conditioned on its prefix. This highlights a mismatch between conventional fixed-codebook quantization and the hierarchical structure implicitly learned by generative recommenders. Motivated by this insight, we propose Adaptive Silhouette Tree (AST), a top-down divisive clustering method that constructs semantic IDs as paths within a tree structure. Unlike prior methods with fixed branching factors, AST dynamically determines the number of branches at each node by maximizing the silhouette coefficient, enabling finer partitions in dense regions and compact groupings in homogeneous ones. We further introduce constrained variants that enforce minimum probability mass during splitting to improve supervision for long-tail items. Extensive experiments on five Amazon Review datasets of varying sizes and domains show that AST significantly outperforms strong baselines. These results demonstrate that aligning semantic ID construction with the inherent hierarchical structure of generative recommenders leads to more effective recommendations.
title: Not All Branches Are Equal: Adaptive Semantic ID Construction for Generative Recommendation

abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.
title: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?

abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

abstract: While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to $2.75\times$ and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from $17.4\%$ to $30.0\%$, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.
title: InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on π-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at github.com/landian60/LiveAsset.
title: LiveAsset: Learning Intent Assets from Corrective Interactions for Agent Runtime Control

abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
title: UTOPI: Efficient Egocentric Long-Video Understanding in AR via User-Guided Token Pre-Compression

abstract: Hydrologic models, including deep learning systems now deployed for operational flood forecasting, are evaluated primarily by how closely their simulated hydrographs match observed streamflow. However, high hydrograph skill does not guarantee physical consistency: in a synthetic calibration experiment, a conceptual model that loses 15% of its water input to an unreported sink still reaches a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.93, and no shared benchmark tests whether models obey fundamental conservation laws. Here we introduce HydroTuring (v0.1.0), a black-box benchmark of 37 physics probes that test mass (24 probes), energy (7) and momentum (6) conservation in hydrologic models. Each probe runs a controlled experiment on forcing generated at run time from a recorded seed and applies binary pass or fail criteria validated against 18 physically exact and 59 deliberately broken reference models. Across 32 evaluated models (3 exact references, 7 AI-based models and 22 process-based models), only the 3 exact references pass every probe among the 28 models scored on 5 or more probes.
